name: Psi4
workload: Single-point B3LYP/6-31G(d) energy of C20 (20 atoms) at 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 cores, timing the whole run of each package with its default convergence criteria and grids and density fitting turned off in Psi4.
claimed_speedup: Psi4 1.3 vs GAMESS-US 2020 in the r2compchem/benchmark-qm table (units not stated, presumably seconds): 726.2 vs 766.2 at 1 core, 372.2 vs 389.1 at 2, 193.2 vs 202.0 at 4, 102.1 vs 130.1 at 8, 60.2 vs 90.1 at 16, i.e. 1.05x to 1.50x faster (ratios derived from page data). Same table: faster than NWChem 7 (726.2 vs 1071.9 at 1 core, 60.2 vs 179.2 at 16), PySCF 1.7 (726.2 vs 1758.9, 60.2 vs 135.5), Firefly 8 and Dalton 2018; faster than Gaussian 16 only at 8 and 16 cores (102.1 vs 117.4, 60.2 vs 68.6); slower than Gaussian 16 at 1 to 4 cores (726.2 vs 535.1 at 1 core).
compiler_and_flags: Psi4 build not described: the repo's compile/README.md lists only 'Build-in Multithreading in Python 3.7' for Psi4 (apparently a prebuilt binary); GAMESS-US built with GNU 4.8.5 and OpenBLAS 0.3.10; Gaussian, Q-Chem and Turbomole builds not described.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 1950X 16-core (32 threads, hyperthreading on), 32 GB DDR4-2666, 2 TB SSD (misc/README.md of the benchmark repo)
tradeoffs: C++ core driven by a Python (Pybind11) front end; free and open source, whereas Gaussian, Q-Chem and Turbomole are commercial. In the benchmark Psi4 was run with density fitting turned off, which is not the way Psi4 is normally used.
caveats: Third-party community benchmark by the r2compchem group: 23 stars, last commit 2020-11-03, no input files in the repo (only three PNG charts), no stated units, one molecule and one method, only Psi4 1.3 (2019; Psi4 is now at v1.11). Per the README only the 'General test' (C20) has data; the MP2, CCSD(T) and SCF-cutoff sections say 'The result is coming'. Defaults differ across packages (Gaussian 16 uses UltraFine grids and 10^-12 integral accuracy, Gaussian 09 FineGrid and 10^-10; GAMESS and Firefly converge on density change; RI/DF is off in ORCA, Psi4 and Turbomole), so it is not an equal-accuracy comparison; the authors state they do not aim to show preference of one package over another. The win over GAMESS is only 5 percent at 1 to 4 cores. Psi4 loses to Gaussian 09, Turbomole 7, Q-Chem 5 and ORCA 4 at every core count (for example 726.2 vs 573.0 for ORCA 4 at 1 core and 60.2 vs 45.5 at 16), and to Gaussian 16 at 1 to 4 cores. Tier B is borderline: it is an independent multi-package shootout with hardware and versions stated, but the benchmark inputs and Psi4 build are not public, so tier C would also be defensible. Corroboration of the PySCF row: pyscf issue #1956 (github.com/pyscf/pyscf/issues/1956, user report, RKS/PBE cc-pVTZ on C6H10 with density fitting, one thread) shows Psi4 at about 45-50 s vs PySCF at about 110 s (and 190 s vs 150 s with density fitting off, where PySCF is faster); the maintainers explained the PySCF slowness (sparse grid code, thread oversubscription; fixed for small systems in PR #1962), and Psi4's integrals are slower for generally contracted sets such as cc-pVTZ. Forum reports (not opened here) also have Psi4 slower than Gaussian and Molpro on other workloads. The category sparse-and-solvers is approximate: Psi4 is a quantum chemistry package and no wave 8 category fits exactly.

name: Quantum++
baseline: Qiskit (QFT) and QuTiP (partial trace, memory ceiling)
workload: Wall-clock time of a quantum Fourier transform and of a partial trace as a function of the number of qubits, single-threaded Quantum++ vs the Python simulators Qiskit and QuTiP, plus the largest qubit count each simulates in 16 GB.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only, no numeric times available: single-core Quantum++ 'over-performs' QuTiP on partial trace and Qiskit 'by a large margin' on QFT; QuTiP is faster than Quantum++ on QFT (it uses sparse matrices); QuTiP runs out of memory after 21 qubits whereas Quantum++ simulates up to 28 qubits.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 6.3, flags not stated in the snippet; Qiskit and QuTiP on Python 3.5
hardware: 8-core x86-64 Debian 9.5, Intel Core i7-7700K 4.20 GHz, 16 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 library built on Eigen with optional OpenMP; the full state vector or density matrix must fit in RAM; Python wrapper pyqpp available.
caveats: Snippet only: the evidence is the PLoS ONE paper 'Quantum++: A modern C++ quantum computing library' (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0208073, arXiv 1412.4704), known to me only through WebSearch result summaries because the PLoS ONE and arXiv hosts are EGRESS_BLOCKED here; nothing was opened and the paper's figures carry the timings, so no times can be quoted. Peer-reviewed, so a verifier who can open it may raise this to B. The paper is by the library's author and the benchmarks date from 2018 (old Qiskit and QuTiP versions, Python 3.5), and the Qiskit and QuTiP versions are unknown; a 2024 independent comparison (arXiv 2401.09076, seen only in a search summary) lists Q++ at 22 qubits for single- and multi-thread double precision, below Qiskit, Qulacs and QuEST, and no newer head-to-head timing was found. The repo's own benchmarks/ directory (Catch2) benchmarks only Quantum++ code, with no other library. Category blas-lapack is approximate (Eigen-based dense linear algebra). The list's URL github.com/vsoftco/qpp now resolves to the softwareQinc/qpp repository (same project, owner renamed); the canonical URL is used here.
